text: No, it is a characteristic of real joy that it never ceases, and never changes into its opposite.
plain: Real joy doesn't fade or flip into its opposite. If it can, it was only pleasure.

text: What hinders us most of all is that we are too readily satisfied with ourselves; if we meet with someone who calls us good men, or sensible men, or holy men, we see ourselves in his description.
plain: Flattery is easy to believe. We start seeing ourselves as the kind words say we are.

text: “All men swear that I am the son of Jupiter, but this wound cries out that I am mortal.”
plain: Everyone can call you a god, and one wound still reminds you that you're human.

text: None of us goes deep below the surface. We skim the top only, and we regard the smattering of time spent in the search for wisdom as enough and to spare for a busy man.
plain: We give wisdom the scraps of our time and call it enough.

text: Joy is the goal which you desire to reach, but you are wandering from the path, if you expect to reach your goal while you are in the midst of riches and official titles,—in other words, if you seek joy in the midst of cares.
plain: You can't reach peace by piling on titles and money. That road runs through more worry.

text: Folly is pursued, and confronted, by peril. It blenches at everything; it is unprepared; it is frightened even by auxiliary troops.
plain: A fool is scared of everything, even his own side. Fear lives in unprepared minds.

text: How small is the amount which will satisfy nature? A very little will send her away contented.
plain: What your body needs is tiny. The rest is appetite.

text: It is not the natural hunger of our bellies that costs us dear, but our solicitous cravings.
plain: Need is cheap. Craving is what costs you.

text: He really lives who is made use of by many; he really lives who makes use of himself.
plain: Living means being useful to others and to yourself.

text: Those men, however, who creep into a hole and grow torpid are no better off in their homes than if they were in their tombs. Right there on the marble lintel of the house of such a man you may inscribe his name, for he has died before he is dead.
plain: Hiding in a hole and going numb is dying early.

text: Let us cease to desire that which we have been desiring.
plain: Stop wanting the same things you've always wanted. They haven't worked.

text: I am endeavouring to live every day as if it were a complete life.
plain: Treat each day as a whole life, not a rehearsal.

text: I do not indeed snatch it up as if it were my last; I do regard it, however, as if it might even be my last.
plain: Don't rush through today. Just don't assume there's another.

text: We must make ready for death before we make ready for life.
plain: Face your end first and you'll live without flinching.

text: Life is well enough furnished, but we are too greedy with regard to its furnishings; something always seems to us lacking, and will always seem lacking.
plain: There's enough. The feeling that something's missing never ends.

text: To have lived long enough depends neither upon our years nor upon our days, but upon our minds.
plain: A full life is about how you think, not how long you last.

text: The man who does something under orders is not unhappy; he is unhappy who does something against his will.
plain: The misery is in doing it unwillingly. Choose the work and it stops being a chain.

text: It is in the power of any man to despise all things, but of no man to possess all things. The shortest cut to riches is to despise riches.
plain: You can't own everything, but you can need nothing. That's the fastest way to rich.

text: We are deceived by those who would have us believe that a multitude of affairs blocks their pursuit of liberal studies; they make a pretence of their engagements, and multiply them, when their engagements are merely with themselves.
plain: Being too busy is mostly an excuse we build ourselves.

text: Let not the eyes be dry when we have lost a friend, nor let them overflow. We may weep, but we must not wail.
plain: Grieve, but don't make a show of it or drown in it.

text: Nothing becomes offensive so quickly as grief; when fresh, it finds someone to console it and attracts one or another to itself; but after becoming chronic, it is ridiculed, and rightly.
plain: Grief that's held onto too long turns stale, even to you.

text: To me, the thought of my dead friends is sweet and appealing. For I have had them as if I should one day lose them; I have lost them as if I have them still.
plain: Love people as if you'll lose them, and you'll keep them after.

text: Let us greedily enjoy our friends, because we do not know how long this privilege will be ours.
plain: Spend time with your people now. You don't know how long you get.

text: You have buried one whom you loved; look about for someone to love. It is better to replace your friend than to weep for him.
plain: Don't mourn alone forever. Go love someone.

text: I should prefer you to abandon grief, rather than have grief abandon you; and you should stop grieving as soon as possible, since, even if you wish to do so, it is impossible to keep it up for a long time.
plain: Put grief down on purpose before it just wears out.

text: Now is the time for you to reflect, not only that all things are mortal, but also that their mortality is subject to no fixed law. Whatever can happen at any time can happen to-day.
plain: Anything that could happen someday could happen today. Plan like it.

text: I want to challenge every hazard; I want to cry: “Why keep me waiting, Fortune? Enter the lists! Behold, I am ready for you!”
plain: Call fate out. Be ready for whatever comes.

text: I want something to overcome, something on which I may test my endurance.
plain: Give me a hard thing to push against. That's how you find your limit.

text: The cures for the spirit also have been discovered by the ancients; but it is our task to learn the method and the time of treatment.
plain: The advice already exists. The work is applying the right piece at the right time.

text: It is either the end, or a process of change. I have no fear of ceasing to exist; it is the same as not having begun.
plain: Death is either nothing or a change. Not being is just like before you were born.

text: Let us be brave in the face of hazards. Let us not fear wrongs, or wounds, or bonds, or poverty.
plain: Don't fear what can be done to you. Wounds, chains, and poverty are survivable.

text: Never shall this flesh drive me to feel fear, or to assume any pretence that is unworthy of a good man.
plain: Don't let your body's comfort make you fake it or fold.

text: A great man can spring from a hovel; so can a beautiful and great soul from an ugly and insignificant body.
plain: Greatness doesn't care where you start or what you look like.

text: That which is not free cannot be honourable; for fear means slavery.
plain: Fear makes you a slave. Nothing done out of fear is worth admiring.

text: I should prefer to be free from torture; but if the time comes when it must be endured, I shall desire that I may conduct myself therein with bravery, honour, and courage.
plain: Nobody asks for hardship, but if it comes, ask to face it well.

text: The conclusion is, not that hardships are desirable, but that virtue is desirable, which enables us patiently to endure hardships.
plain: Don't chase pain. Build the strength to take it.

text: Clothe yourself with a hero’s courage, and withdraw for a little space from the opinions of the common man. Form a proper conception of the image of virtue, a thing of exceeding beauty and grandeur; this image is not to be worshipped by us with incense or garlands, but with sweat and blood.
plain: Ignore the crowd for a while. Greatness is paid for in sweat, not applause.

text: If you have nothing to stir you up and rouse you to action, nothing which will test your resolution by its threats and hostilities; if you recline in unshaken comfort, it is not tranquillity; it is merely a flat calm.
plain: Comfort without challenge isn't peace. It's stagnation.

text: “I should prefer that Fortune keep me in her camp rather than in the lap of luxury. If I am tortured, but bear it bravely, all is well; if I die, but die bravely, it is also well.”
plain: Better to be tested by fate than spoiled by comfort. Bear it bravely and it's fine either way.

text: To boast of our retirement is but idle self-seeking.
plain: Announcing your retreat from the world is just another way to be noticed.

text: When you withdraw from the world your business is to talk with yourself, not to have men talk about you.
plain: Alone time is for talking to yourself honestly, not for being talked about.

text: Do just what people are fond of doing when they talk about their neighbours,—speak ill of yourself when by yourself; then you will become accustomed both to speak and to hear the truth.
plain: Criticize yourself in private the way people criticize others. You'll get used to the truth.

text: You are mistaken if you think that you will get any assistance from this quarter; it is not a physician that dwells here, but a sick man.
plain: I'm not a cure, I'm a patient working on it too. Don't put me on a pedestal.

text: Would that in earlier days you had been minded to follow this purpose! Would that we were not discussing the happy life in plain view of death!
plain: It's a shame to start living wisely only when death is in sight. Start now.

text: Let us do what men are wont to do when they are late in setting forth, and wish to make up for lost time by increasing their speed—let us ply the spur.
plain: Started late? Go faster, not slower.

text: To be able to hold your spirit in check, you must first stop the runaway flight of the body.
plain: To calm your mind, stop running around.

text: There is no evil that does not offer inducements.
plain: Every vice comes with a reward. That's why it works on you.

text: Vices tempt you by the rewards which they offer; but in the life of which I speak, you must live without being paid.
plain: Vices pay you right now. Discipline asks you to work for nothing up front.

text: Scarcely will a whole life-time suffice to bring our vices into subjection and to make them accept the yoke, swollen as they are by long-continued indulgence; and still less, if we cut into our brief span by any interruptions.
plain: Beating bad habits takes a lifetime of steady work. Every break makes it longer.

text: Give your eyes time to unlearn what they have seen, and your ears to grow accustomed to more wholesome words.
plain: Change what you look at and listen to, and your cravings change.

text: Would you be free from the restraint of your body? Live in it as if you were about to leave it.
plain: Live loose. Hold nothing, including your body, like it's permanent.

text: Our souls have been made ready to meet poverty; but our riches have held out. We have armed ourselves to scorn pain; but we have had the good fortune to possess sound and healthy bodies, and so have never been forced to put this virtue to the test.
plain: Comfort hides how untested you are. Your strength hasn't been tried yet.

text: Humanity is well situated, because no man is unhappy except by his own fault.
plain: Nobody is truly unhappy unless they let themselves be.

text: When a man does not know what harbour he is making for, no wind is the right wind.
plain: If you don't know where you're going, no luck will help.

text: Our plans miscarry because they have no aim.
plain: Plans fail because there's no target.

text: The reason we make mistakes is because we all consider the parts of life, but never life as a whole.
plain: We fuss over pieces of life and forget to ask what the whole thing is for.

text: There is nothing that does not have its old age; the intervals are merely unequal at which Nature sends forth all these things towards the same goal.
plain: Everything ages and ends. Nothing is special enough to be exempt.

text: These actions are not essentially difficult; it is we ourselves that are soft and flabby.
plain: The thing isn't hard. We've gone soft.

text: It matters not only what you see, but with what eyes you see it; our souls are too dull of vision to perceive the truth.
plain: How you see matters more than what you see.

text: It is not a cause for wonder that one is not tossed about when the weather is calm; reserve your wonderment for cases where a man is lifted up when all others sink, and keeps his footing when all others are prostrate.
plain: Calm in calm weather proves nothing. Respect the one standing when everyone else is down.

text: What element of evil is there in torture and in the other things which we call hardships? It seems to me that there is this evil,—that the mind sags, and bends, and collapses.
plain: Hardship's real damage is when your mind gives out.

text: Allow any man who so desires to insult you and work you wrong; but if only virtue dwells with you, you will suffer nothing.
plain: Insults only hurt if you give up your own character.

text: There remains much more of the road than we have put behind us; but the greater part of progress is the desire to progress.
plain: Most of the road is still ahead, and wanting to move is half of moving.

text: Let us see to it that all time belongs to us. This, however, cannot be unless first of all our own selves begin to belong to us.
plain: To own your time, you first have to own yourself.

text: Neither the Persians, nor the far-off Medes, nor any warlike race that lies beyond the Dahae; not these, but greed, ambition, and the fear of death that has conquered the conquerors of the world.
plain: The real enemies to conquer are greed, ambition, and fear of death.

text: To a luxurious man, a simple life is a penalty; to a lazy man, work is punishment; the dandy pities the diligent man; to the slothful, studies are torture.
plain: Hard is relative. What feels like punishment is just what you're soft about.

text: Then, too, we keep adjourning our own cases, saying: “As soon as I am done with this, I shall settle down to hard work,” or: “If I ever set this troublesome matter in order, I shall devote myself to study.”
plain: "After this one thing, I'll start" never ends. There's always another thing.

text: Now all that which the crowd gapes after, ebbs and flows. Fortune gives us nothing which we can really own.
plain: What the crowd chases rises and falls. Fortune never actually gives you anything to keep.

text: That is the trouble with every sort of ambition; it does not look back. Nor is it ambition alone that is fickle, but also every sort of craving, because it always begins where it ought to end.
plain: Ambition never looks back at how far you've come. Craving starts where it should stop.

text: The gods are not disdainful or envious; they open the door to you; they lend a hand as you climb.
plain: The way up is open. Nothing's blocking you but you.

text: Whoever has largely surrendered himself to the power of Fortune has made for himself a huge web of disquietude, from which he cannot get free; if one would win a way to safety, there is but one road,—to despise externals and to be contented with that which is honourable.
plain: Handing your peace to fortune builds a trap. The only way out is needing less from outside.

text: The most sensible man, therefore, as soon as he sees the dole being brought in, runs from the theatre; for he knows that one pays a high price for small favours. No one will grapple with him on the way out, or strike him as he departs; the quarrelling takes place where the prizes are.
plain: The smart one leaves the scramble. The fighting is always where the prizes are.

text: Few men have been permitted to lay aside prosperity gently. The rest all fall, together with the things amid which they have come into eminence, and they are weighted down by the very things which had before exalted them.
plain: Few people leave success gracefully. The rest get crushed by what raised them.

text: Let us use these things, but not boast of them, and let us use them sparingly, as if they were given for safe-keeping and will be withdrawn.
plain: Use what you have lightly. It's on loan.

text: Let everything of this nature be added to us, and not stick fast to us, so that, if it is withdrawn, it may come away without tearing off any part of us.
plain: Own things so loosely that losing them costs you nothing of yourself.

text: We should fortify ourselves against such calamities. But no wall can be erected against Fortune which she cannot take by storm; let us strengthen our inner defences. If the inner part be safe, man can be attacked, but never captured.
plain: Fortune can breach any wall. Make the inside strong and you can be hit but not taken.

text: Love reason! The love of reason will arm you against the greatest hardships.
plain: A clear mind is your best armor.

text: Like birds, who cower even at the whirr of an empty sling, we are distracted by mere sounds as well as by blows.
plain: We flinch at noise as much as at actual hits.

text: Do you ask why virtue needs nothing? Because it is pleased with what it has, and does not lust after that which it has not. Whatever is enough is abundant in the eyes of virtue.
plain: Being content with what you have makes you complete.

text: Past and future are both absent; we feel neither of them. But there can be no pain except as the result of what you feel.
plain: Past and future aren't here. You only hurt from what you feel now.

text: Let this be the kernel of my idea: let us say what we feel, and feel what we say; let speech harmonize with life.
plain: Say what you feel. Live what you say.

text: That man has fulfilled his promise who is the same person both when you see him and when you hear him.
plain: Be the same person in private and in public.

text: Our words should aim not to please, but to help.
plain: Don't try to impress. Try to help.

text: Why do you tickle my ears? Why do you entertain me? There is other business at hand; I am to be cauterized, operated upon, or put on a diet.
plain: I don't need to be entertained. I need the hard treatment.

text: When shall you learn all that there is to learn? When shall you so plant in your mind that which you have learned, that it cannot escape? When shall you put it all into practice?
plain: When do you stop learning and start doing?

text: He is not happy who only knows them, but he who does them.
plain: Knowing isn't enough. Do it.

text: We hasten towards virtue while hampered by vices. I am ashamed to say it; but we worship that which is honourable only in so far as we have time to spare.
plain: We chase the good life with bad habits dragging us, and only give it spare time.

text: Undisturbed by fears, unspoiled by pleasures, we shall be afraid neither of death nor of the gods; we shall know that death is no evil and that the gods are not powers of evil.
plain: Without fear or cheap pleasures, death and the gods stop being threats.

text: And it is a priceless good to be master of oneself.
plain: Mastering yourself is the best thing you can own.
